intro: Before Violetta’s party begins, Verdi gives us the frailty of her high violin music and the warmth of her love song. Toscanini conducts the New York Philharmonic in this small, piercing portrait.

sections.label: Intro · High divided violins
sections.mNote: Quiet violin chords hang above an empty bass register

sections.label: A · Violetta’s love melody
sections.mNote: The strings sing in E major above regularly spaced bass notes

sections.label: A′ · Cellos beneath violin lace
sections.mNote: Cellos and bassoon carry the tune beneath quick violin decoration

sections.label: Coda · The last quiet E
sections.mNote: Short phrases dwindle into an E-major chord

cues.title: Violins without a floor
cues.text: Only the violins begin, divided into small groups and marked ppp. Their high notes hang over silence where the bass ought to be. When violas and a solo cello join, the melody acquires a warmer, human reach.
cues.evidence: Verdi, La traviata, Ricordi full score, 1914, plate 113958, p. 1: eight solo players in each violin section, divided; viola and solo cello enter later. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6c/IMSLP514870-PMLP16223-Verdi_-_La_traviata.pdf.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Verdi the morning after
cues.text: On 7 March 1853, Verdi writes to Emanuele Muzio about the previous night’s première in Venice: “La traviata last night a failure. Was the fault mine or the singers’? Time will tell.”
cues.evidence: Verdi to Emanuele Muzio, 7 March 1853, English translation quoted in the performance history at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_traviata. La Fenice première, 6 March, also documented by English National Opera: https://www.eno.org/discover-opera/articles/an-introduction-to-la-traviata/.

cues.title: Love me, Alfredo
cues.text: The strings sing the broad E-major melody that Violetta later gives to Alfredo: “Amami, Alfredo” — “Love me, Alfredo.” In Act II she sings it just before leaving him. Here the tune arrives without words, supported by the orchestra’s gently repeated chords.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, Prelude, p. 2, love theme; Piave’s libretto, Act II, Violetta’s Amami, Alfredo before her departure. The dramatic context and prelude themes are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_traviata. Translation ours.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The song beneath the lace
cues.text: The cellos and bassoon keep the long melody while the first violins decorate it with quick, detached notes. Clarinet adds another singing line. The upper strings sparkle, but the cellos still have the words that matter.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, pp. 3–5: cello and first bassoon melody, clarinet line, divided first-violin semiquavers, repeated inner-string chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A play seen in Paris
cues.text: In February 1852 Verdi, living in Paris with Giuseppina Strepponi, sees Dumas fils’s new play La Dame aux camélias. Eleven months later he writes to Cesare De Sanctis that his subject for Venice is “of the age”, one another composer might shun for its costumes, its period and “a thousand other clumsy scruples”.
cues.evidence: Oreste Bossini, “Violetta, o la moderna Maddalena”, Teatro Lirico di Cagliari programme essay: Verdi’s letter of 21 January 1852 from Paris, the play’s performance there in February 1852, and his letter to Cesare De Sanctis of 1 January 1853, “Un soggetto dell’epoca. Un altro forse non l’avrebbe fatto per i costumi, pei tempi e per altri mille goffi scrupoli” (translation ours): https://www.liricocagliari.it/archivio/media/12/85725238805832/2020_violetta_maddalena.pdf . René Weis, Royal Opera House: the play’s première at the Vaudeville on 2 February 1852, where Verdi and Strepponi probably first met the story: https://www.rbo.org.uk/news/the-real-traviata-the-tragic-true-story-that-inspired-la-traviata

cues.title: A quiet E major
cues.text: The phrases shorten. Verdi writes allargando, then diminuendo and morendo — dying away. The first violins keep their little repeated notes almost to the end; the bass moves from B to E, and the prelude closes softly before the party can begin.
cues.evidence: Ricordi full score, p. 6, final systems: allargando, diminuendo, morendo and E-major cadence. The following stage scene begins with Violetta’s party.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A bass beneath the love song
transitions.how: The high violin phrase descends. Regular bass notes and short wind chords establish E major; the first violins, violas and cellos take up the love melody together, con espressione. For the first time, the tune has the whole string section beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi full score, pp. 1–2: descending end of the introduction, new bass and wind accompaniment, con espressione string melody in E major.

transitions.title: The melody passes below the violins
transitions.how: A short cello line links the two statements. The cellos then sing the E-major melody with the first bassoon, while divided first violins break into detached semiquavers above them. Second violins and violas repeat their chords; the bass maintains its spaced notes.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi full score, p. 3, cello link and decorated restatement, continuing on pp. 4–5.

transitions.title: The violin figures run out
transitions.how: The melody contracts into short figures exchanged with the wind. At allargando the bass reaches B, preparing the final E-major chord. Verdi follows with diminuendo and morendo. The violin semiquavers continue through the softening chords, then stop at the last sustained E.
transitions.evidence: Ricordi full score, p. 6, final cadential systems and printed expressive markings.

source.title: Verdi, La traviata, full score (Milan: G. Ricordi, 1914, plate 113958; Dover reprint)
source.locator: No. 1, Preludio, printed pp. 1–6; bars placed between the file’s section times

timeline.note: Eight solo violins, divided, in the highest register; nothing else sounds.
Violas and cellos enter; a solo clarinet and horn join the violins.
Cantabile in E major: violins sing over soft repeated wind notes and a plucked bass.
The tune moves to violas and cellos, supported by clarinet and bassoon, as the violins decorate.
A solo horn joins; the clarinet sings above the divided violins.
The decoration thickens: violin trills and figures with short wind phrases over the cellos.
Quiet close: allargando, diminuendo, morendo; the whole ensemble dying away.

composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: He could make a catchy tenor tune sound like a death sentence simply by letting the wrong man hear it.
facts: Provesi in Busseto; private lessons with Lavigna after Milan’s Conservatoire rejected him
Milan · Venice · Florence · Rome · Naples · Paris · St Petersburg · Cairo
Piave, Cammarano and Boito were his principal collaborators
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred music, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Milan’s Conservatoire turned Giuseppe Verdi down in 1832. Antonio Barezzi, a merchant from Busseto who had helped pay for his move to Milan, kept supporting him, and Verdi studied privately with Vincenzo Lavigna, formerly a musician at La Scala. He learnt counterpoint and went to the theatre. Four years later he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took a municipal musical post in Busseto. His patrons were people who had heard him play, watched him grow up and put their own money behind him.

His parents kept an inn and shop at Le Roncole, where he was born in 1813. He learnt the organ locally, then studied with Ferdinando Provesi in nearby Busseto. Oberto, his first opera, reached La Scala in 1839 and earned him further commissions. His daughter Virginia had died in 1838; his son Icilio died in 1839, and Margherita in June 1840. That September the theatre presented his comedy Un giorno di regno. It failed. Verdi was twenty-six and had lost his wife and both children.
